flawed_step: The step from "X is independent of Y and X is independent of Z" to "X is independent of the pair (Y,Z)" can't be justified. Independence from each variable separately only says P(X∈A, Y∈B) = P(X∈A)P(Y∈B) and P(X∈A, Z∈C) = P(X∈A)P(Z∈C). It says nothing about the joint events {Y∈B, Z∈C}, so the factorization P(X∈A, Y∈B, Z∈C) = P(X∈A)P(Y∈B, Z∈C) doesn't follow. Because this step fails, the conclusion about Y+Z fails too.
counterexample: Let Y and Z be independent fair bits (values 0 or 1), and set X = Y XOR Z. Then X is a fair bit, and for every a and b, P(X=a, Y=b) = P(Z = a XOR b, Y=b) = 1/4 = P(X=a)P(Y=b). So X is independent of Y, and by symmetry X is independent of Z. But X is a function of (Y,Z), so it is not independent of the pair. It is not independent of Y+Z either: X=1 exactly when Y+Z=1, so P(X=1, Y+Z=1) = 1/2, while P(X=1)P(Y+Z=1) = 1/4.
assessment_summary: The statement is false because independence from each variable separately (pairwise independence) does not give independence from the pair. The proof attempt breaks at the first step, going from separate independence to independence from (Y,Z). The XOR example shows this: X is independent of Y and of Z, but is completely determined by (Y,Z) and depends on Y+Z. The claim would only hold with extra assumptions, such as X being independent of (Y,Z) jointly.
